name: Thylodrias contractus
intro: I started my odd beetle culture with about 30 living larvae that I recovered from a damaged insect collection in February 2026. The beetles were especially common around moths and orthopterans. By mid-March several had matured. Two months later I nearly wrote the culture off before I spotted the tiny larvae of the next generation.

sections.title: Larvae
sections.text:
I first look beneath damaged specimens and in the loose debris around them. That was where I could recover living larvae among the remains. For a new colony I would move some of the material on which the larvae have already been feeding to a separate, close-fitting container. I considered crickets as a substitute for the dried insects. The damage I actually observed was to moths and orthopterans in the collection. I keep a live culture well away from pinned specimens.
Several larvae had matured during the two weeks before my March 15 check. On May 19, small larvae finally caught my eye in the enclosure. I would keep an apparently quiet container and examine the remaining food under magnification before starting over. A laboratory study found a typical life cycle of 12.8 months, with individuals ranging from about six and a half months to more than 46 months. My February founders were already larvae when I collected them, so their March emergence tells me when the first adults appeared, but not their total age.

sections.title: Adults
sections.text: An adult female can look so much like a larva that it is easy to overlook her during a count. Females are wingless throughout adult life. Males have wing covers, but the hind wings underneath vary considerably in size. I look for both forms when checking for maturity, then use the appearance of a new size class of small larvae as evidence of reproduction.

sources.title: Biggs, Herrmann and Cognato (2022), North American dermestids
